title: Reinsurance & Commercial Lines
breadcrumb: Industries > Insurance & Risk > Reinsurance & Commercial Lines
meta_description: Reinsurance and commercial lines run on submission intake, bordereaux reconciliation, treaty structures and cat exposure accumulation. Dataq Software engineers the data plane, decision layer and evidence systems behind them.

blocks.x: Reinsurance and specialty commercial books trade in complexity: treaty structures layered on treaty structures, facultative risks priced on judgment and thin data, bordereaux that arrive as spreadsheets in a dozen shapes, and capital models whose answers are only as current as the exposures feeding them. The money moves between cedants, reinsurers and brokers, which means every data gap is also a relationship gap — a settlement that stalls because two parties read different numbers, a recovery missed because the notification window closed quietly. This page is the engineering picture of that wholesale machine as Dataq Software sees it: how placement, cession, recovery and settlement actually run, where each stage leaks money or trust, and the six deep builds that shorten cycles and harden evidence on the ground between counterparties.
How the wholesale machine actually runs

Reinsurance and specialty commercial books are wholesale markets built on borrowed balance sheets, and the machine starts at placement. A broker assembles a submission — the slip, the statement of fact, the exposure schedules, the loss history — and markets it to underwriters whose appetite is a mix of written guide and desk judgment. Quotes carry basis-of-terms that later become the dispute. On bind, the contract certainty clock starts: documentation must follow the agreement within the timeliness rules the market and its regulators expect. Every treaty written — quota share, surplus, per-risk or aggregate excess of loss — is a promise whose arithmetic will be tested by bordereaux for years.

After bind, the machine turns cessional. Cedants report premium and loss through bordereaux, quarterly or monthly, in formats and qualities that vary by counterparty; the treaty administration system reconciles them against terms, calculates balances, and drives settlement through closing statements and cash. Ceded claims — especially large losses — open recovery cases with notification windows, evidence requirements and commutation possibilities. Catastrophe events test accumulation: the per-event and aggregate views that decide whether the retro program attaches, erodes or holds. And retrocession closes the loop, reinsuring the reinsurer with the same mechanics one layer up.

Underneath, the actuarial and capital engine prices the next cycle and proves this one. Pricing actuaries run experience ratings and burning-cost analyses on loss triangles that must be assembled from the same messy bordereaux; capital teams feed exposure and loss data into Solvency II internal models and ORSA processes; runoff teams manage books whose claims will develop for another decade. The quiet truth of this sub-industry is that every one of those functions reads the same underlying flows — and where the flows are spreadsheets, every function inherits the same reconciliation debt and passes it downstream.

Programs here succeed or fail on how honestly the estate is mapped before anything is built. Dataq Software starts every reinsurance and commercial engagement by naming the systems, their owners, their change cadences and their data contracts — and in this sub-industry the map must include counterparties, because the data estate is partly other people's systems. blocks.x: Where the margin leaks

Ask reinsurance underwriting, actuarial and operations leaders where the money leaks and the answers converge on the same eight places, described in their own words. Dataq Software scores each of them in your estate during the diagnostic, because the leak that dominates a cat treaty book is often minor in a specialty facultative portfolio — and the trust leak is rarely measured at all.

items: Bordereaux reconciliation as an analyst occupation

Premium and loss bordereaux arrive in formats and qualities no schema anticipated, so reconciliation consumes analysts quarter after quarter, exceptions queue by age rather than by risk, and the data-quality issues that cause them stay hidden inside totals that still net out.
Settlement disputes resting on bilateral numbers

Closing statements are produced by each party from its own reconciliation, so a dispute becomes a comparison of two private spreadsheets with no shared evidence chain. Settlement stretches, cash stays parked, and the relationship absorbs friction nobody prices.
Ceded recoveries claimed late or not at all

Large-loss notification windows, evidence requirements and commutation options live in the treaty documents nobody queries. Recoveries are under-claimed when notice goes out late, under-documented when the evidence pack is thin, and the recoverable asset is softer than the reconciliation suggests.
Accumulation blind spots before the event

Exposure data quality — geocoding, secondary modifiers, valuation basis — goes unverified until a cat model run exposes it. Per-event and aggregate views lag the in-force book by weeks, and the retro program's attachment points are monitored from reports rather than from data.
Pricing actuaries assembling instead of analysing

Experience ratings and burning-cost analyses start with extract-and-reconcile spreadsheet work that consumes the analyst quarter. Pricing rationale lives in documents the next renewal cannot query, and the strategy conversation happens on numbers assembled the week before.
Capital models fed by stale data

Internal model runs wait on exposure and claims feeds assembled manually, so the SCR and ORSA answers describe last quarter's book. Lineage between exposure, claims and capital exists as institutional memory, and every model change becomes a data archaeology project.
Appetite drifting desk by desk

Specialty commercial underwriting runs on judgment with variable evidence, so appetite drifts by desk and by broker relationship. The guide says one thing, the written book says another, and nobody can measure the gap until the loss ratio reports it.
Runoff surprises in legacy books

Reserve triangulation for runoff portfolios runs on extracts assembled by hand, claims inventory lives in old systems, and LPT or commutation diligence means building a data room from scratch. Legacy books close slower and more expensively than their economics require.

blocks.x: The pattern across all eight leaks: this is the only insurance market where the data estate is partly owned by counterparties, so every data gap is also a trust gap. The builds that pay first are the ones that make two parties read the same numbers — which is why bordereaux and settlement evidence lead.
How Dataq Software works reinsurance and commercial lines

Dataq Software builds inside the estate you already run — the treaty administration system, the submission workbench, the capital suite, the broker portals — not against them. We do not arrive with a replacement platform or a strategy deck that ends where the hard part begins. The engagement model is engineering-first: a two-week diagnostic that baselines one workflow end to end — bordereaux reconciliation, placement turnaround, ceded recovery or capital data feeds — then a scoped build that ships behind your change process, your model-risk framework and your counterparty confidentiality obligations from the first sprint.

Three engineering commitments shape everything we deliver in this sub-industry. First, every automated decision carries replay: reconciliation results, pricing inputs, recovery demands and settlement proposals are stored with their evidence, so a dispute twelve months later is a retrieval of what both sides saw. Second, every generative component is permission-aware and citation-bound — grounded in your treaty documents, underwriting guides and the structured case record, never the open internet, with counterparty confidentiality enforced at the retrieval layer. Third, every build lands with its evidence layer: the artifacts a supervisory review, an audit or a counterparty dispute will ask for are generated continuously by the system.

The commercial model follows the same logic: where the metric is clean we contract against the delta with the baseline locked during the diagnostic, and where it is confounded the feasibility read says so. The published record behind this approach sits on this exact ground — a European specialty reinsurer cut bordereaux reconciliation effort 74% with automated settlement evidence in Dataq Software's record — because the reconciliation engine is where wholesale books pay first, and the settlement evidence it produces is what keeps the delta from eroding back.
The builds: six deep engineering services for reinsurance and commercial lines

The catalog below is the whole of our reinsurance and commercial lines practice. Each build is named for the workflow it changes, sized in the diagnostic, and shipped with the controls its regulator and counterparties will expect. None of them require replacing the treaty core; every one of them requires treating counterparty data as a governed asset rather than an attachment.
1. Submission intelligence and the placement workbench

The placement build attacks the front of the machine, where broker submissions arrive as documents and die in email. Document intelligence classifies slips, statements of fact, exposure schedules and loss histories; extracts the risk facts with confidence scores; and drafts a structured risk summary the underwriter checks rather than assembles. Appetite matching scores each submission against the underwriting guide and the desk's demonstrated book, flagging in-appetite candidates for fast lanes and routing out-of-appetite referrals with the reasoning attached. Quote construction pulls basis-of-terms from structured templates so the quote that binds is the quote you can defend.

The workbench then manages the clock: quote turnaround measured per broker and per desk, contract certainty timelines tracked from agreement to documentation, referral leakage monitored as a first-class metric. Every quote and declination writes to the replay store with its inputs and reason codes, so a conduct question or a broker dispute is answered from the record the decision made. The measurable deltas are quote turnaround, hit ratio on in-appetite submissions and the documentation timeliness that contract certainty rules — and broker relationships — depend on.
2. The bordereaux engine — ingestion, reconciliation and settlement evidence

The bordereaux build replaces the analyst occupation with an engine. Ingestion accepts whatever each counterparty sends — spreadsheets, ACORD messages, portal exports — and normalises it against a schema registry that learns counterparty quirks as versioned rules rather than as tribal knowledge. Quality scoring grades every file on completeness, consistency and term-alignment before reconciliation; the reconciliation itself matches premium, loss, natural-return-premium adjustments and reinstatements against the treaty terms as code, and exceptions route to counterparty-specific queues with the mismatch located, not a vague variance.

Settlement sits on the same foundation: closing statements generate from the reconciled record with the evidence chain attached, so both parties read the same numbers — and the dispute, when it happens, is a lookup rather than a negotiation. Collateral and letters of credit are monitored against exposure movements so security tracks the book it secures. In the published record, a European specialty reinsurer cut reconciliation effort 74% with this build; the measurable deltas are reconciliation hours, exception age and settlement cycle time per treaty.
3. Cat accumulation and the capital data platform

The accumulation build makes exposure legible before the event. An exposure data quality program verifies geocoding, secondary modifiers and valuation basis continuously rather than annually; vendor cat model feeds integrate through contract-tested pipelines instead of file drops; and per-event, per-peril and aggregate accumulation views refresh with the in-force book, so the retro program's attachment and erosion are monitored from data rather than from quarterly reports. Event response reads the same views: footprints join to exposure within hours, and the notification obligations in the retro treaties track themselves.

The capital platform feeds Solvency II internal models and ORSA processes from governed pipelines: exposure and claims data with lineage from source to model, run cycles shortened because the data assembly is no longer manual, and scenario management that answers the supervisory question — what changed and why — as a query. The measurable deltas are exposure data completeness, accumulation refresh latency and the internal model run cycle that currently waits on spreadsheets.
4. Ceded claims recovery and large-loss case management

The recovery build treats ceded claims as a clock-and-evidence business, which is what they are. Large losses are detected in the claim stream and matched to the treaties that respond; notification windows compute automatically from treaty terms and track as hard deadlines, because late notice is the silent killer of recoveries. The recovery case assembles itself — treaty terms, loss notices, adjuster reports, financials, expert evidence — and the recoverable is tracked from notice to collection, with commutation candidates scored on economics and evidence readiness rather than on fatigue.

Large-loss case management gives the complex claims the structure they need: coverage questions, counsel and expert coordination, reserve development and settlement strategy tracked in one case record instead of an email thread. Every recovery decision writes to the replay store, so a disputed recovery is answered from the record — the notice date, the evidence pack, the treaty clause — rather than from memory. The measurable deltas are recovery capture rate, days-to-notify and the commutation value that currently leaks because nobody priced it.
5. The pricing actuarial workbench — treaty analytics

The pricing build gives the actuarial function its quarter back. Experience-rating pipelines assemble loss triangles, development factors and exposure adjustments from the governed lakehouse instead of from extract-and-reconcile spreadsheets; burning-cost analyses, rate-on-line calculations and loss-ratio projections run as reproducible pipelines with versioned assumptions; and pricing rationale — the model, the data window, the judgment calls — is stored as structured record per treaty, so next year's renewal starts from last year's reasoning rather than from a document hunt.

Portfolio steering rides the same workbench: treaty-by-treaty adequacy, retro efficiency and capacity allocation analysed on current data, with renewal strategy prepared as evidence rather than assembled as slides. Model governance is built in — pricing models register with their evaluation results, challengers run on shadow data, and the replay store answers the explainability question the EU AI Act class of regulation asks. The measurable deltas are pricing turnaround per treaty, renewal retention where retention is wanted, and adequacy at renewal measured rather than assumed.
6. Runoff and legacy portfolio operations — closing books honestly

The runoff build industrialises the end of the book. Reserve triangulation pipelines assemble the triangles from governed data so movement between reviews is explained by the record rather than by estimate drift; claims inventory is digitized and classified so the book's remaining work is countable; and commutation candidates are screened on economics, evidence readiness and counterparty posture — because closing a book is a negotiation, and negotiations are won on preparation.

For LPT deals and legacy transactions, the same machinery becomes diligence support: data rooms assemble from governed marts rather than from a team extracting extracts for months, reserve and claims-quality evidence is produced from the systems rather than summarised for them, and post-transaction administration runs on the same pipelines the diligence used — so the buyer's questions and the servicing reality are the same numbers. The measurable deltas are reserve review cycle time, diligence preparation effort and the runoff expense ratio that readiness compresses.

blocks.x: The data plane: from counterparty spreadsheets to governed flows

Every decision gap in reinsurance traces back to a data gap, and the gaps here are structural: the estate is partly owned by counterparties, the formats are negotiated one spreadsheet at a time, and the treaty terms that govern everything live in PDFs. The data plane build handles all three. Bordereaux, broker submissions and cat feeds land through the contract layer with schema validation and quality scoring; treaty terms are extracted into a structured term library that the reconciliation and recovery services query as code; and the exposure-claims-capital join is built once as a governed model rather than rebuilt per analysis.

Governance is engineered, not asserted. Every feed carries a schema contract with a named owner, a freshness SLA and a quality score that trends over time — because counterparty data quality is a managed relationship, not a weather condition. Confidentiality is enforced at the retrieval layer: counterparty A never sees counterparty B's data through the index, and the access logs prove it. Every downstream consumer — reconciliation, pricing, recovery, capital — reads through the contract layer, so a counterparty format change fails loudly at the contract instead of silently inside a settlement.

blocks.x: The decision layer: reconciliation, replay and reason codes

A wholesale book runs on decisions whose disputes are expensive and whose evidence is bilateral: a reconciliation adjustment, a recovery demand, a quote's basis-of-terms, a settlement proposal. The decision layer we build treats those tails as first-class requirements. Every decision records its inputs — the bordereau rows, the treaty clauses, the model versions, the judgment calls — in a replay store that answers a counterparty dispute or a supervisory question as a query. When another party asks why the balance moved, both sides can read the same evidence chain instead of comparing private spreadsheets.

Champion/challenger governance is built in rather than bolted on: pricing and reconciliation challengers run on shadow data with performance tracked in the registry your model-risk function owns, promotions pass through the gates your framework already defines, and rollbacks are rehearsed rather than improvised. The same decision layer hosts reconciliation, settlement proposals, treaty pricing and recovery scoring, so the governance surface is one registry and one replay store — instead of four platforms with four audit stories and a dispute process that relies on whoever kept the better spreadsheet.
The agentic layer: digital workers with audit trails

The backlog work in a wholesale book — bordereaux matching, exception triage, submission summarisation, recovery demand assembly, diligence data rooms — follows patterns an agentic workforce can absorb without touching settlement authority. Dataq Software's agent platform runs digital workers with explicit role scopes: the tools they may call, the counterparties' data they may read, the actions that require a human checkpoint and the budget of work per run. Every run logs its steps, tool calls and outputs to the same evidence store the human workflow uses, so an agent's file is auditable exactly like an analyst's.

Where generative agents add leverage — summarising submissions for underwriters, drafting recovery demands from the structured case record, assembling settlement evidence packs — the pattern is grounded generation with citation obligations and human authorship of record. Agents never settle, never sign statements, never send counterparty communications without review, and never change a reconciled balance; they move the work to the decision point and stop. The capacity story is measured in cleared exceptions per analyst per day, which is how operations leaders who sponsor these programs justify them upward.

The regulatory surface of reinsurance and specialty commercial is supervisory, bilateral and increasingly algorithmic: capital and reserving regimes, contract certainty and market conduct rules, counterparty financial-crime duties, confidentiality obligations across borders, and AI governance reaching into pricing and underwriting. Dataq Software's answer is the evidence layer — the artifacts a reviewer, a counterparty or a supervisor will ask for are generated continuously by the systems themselves. blocks.x: Integration engineering: the estate stays, the contracts change

Reinsurance estates are small in system count and enormous in counterparty complexity, and the fastest way to fail a program is to promise greenfield. Our integration posture is contractual: we define schema contracts with each system owner, land data through CDC and governed APIs, write back through the treaty administration and settlement interfaces your change process already controls, and keep every new component independently deployable behind feature flags. The treaty core is not replaced; it is supplied with structured terms and reconciled data, and drained of the matching work it was never good at.

The counterparty and vendor chain gets the same treatment. Broker portals, cat model vendors, capital modeling suites and market infrastructure sit behind an abstraction layer with contract tests, so a vendor or counterparty change is a configuration change with a migration runbook rather than a re-platform. Where a legacy component must stay, the offload pattern applies: the batch cycle keeps posting, while the decision surfaces read from the governed flows the offload produces. This is unglamorous work, and it is the reason the builds above hold up across counterparties instead of across a pilot.

blocks.x: The team and the operating rhythm

A reinsurance build team is small and senior: a lead engineer who has run decision systems in wholesale insurance, data engineers who own the contract layer and the counterparty feeds, ML engineers who own scoring and evaluation, a controls engineer who owns the evidence and confidentiality layer, and a domain lead who has run treaty administration, ceded claims or capital reporting in production estates. Agentic-workflow specialists join for the bordereaux and diligence builds, and an actuarial SME keeps the pricing build honest to the renewal calendar. The team works to your release calendar and your gate vocabulary from the first week.

The rhythm is the same at every client: weekly operations review on the workflow's own telemetry, fortnightly gate submissions to change and model-risk, quarterly challenger reviews aligned to the settlement and renewal calendars, and an incident practice that treats the replay store, the term library and the evidence layer as production-critical systems — because by the second quarter, they are. Escalations go to named engineers, not to a queue.
Failure modes we design against

Programs like these fail in known ways, and in wholesale books the failure modes are bilateral: a build that works for your side of the trade but not the counterparty's creates friction rather than margin. We name them in the feasibility read and design against them explicitly, because a program that cannot survive its second quarter is not worth starting.

blocks.x: Questions reinsurance and specialty leaders ask us

items: Do we need to replace our treaty administration system first?

No. The builds consume streams from the treaty core, counterparty feeds and broker portals, and write back through your interfaces. The structured term library and the reconciliation engine do the heavy lifting; the core stays what it is.
Will counterparties accept machine-generated settlement evidence?

Acceptance follows the evidence chain, not the format: closing statements generated from a reconciled record with lookups per line are easier to audit than a private spreadsheet. In the published record, disputes declined because both parties finally read the same numbers.
How does this pass Solvency II and internal model review?

The capital platform ships with lineage from source data to model input, run-cycle telemetry and assumption evidence. Model changes register with evaluation results, and the ORSA narrative is supported by data the supervisor can trace — which is what the review actually tests.
What happens to our reconciliation analysts?

The engine takes the matching; analysts take the exceptions, the counterparty relationships and the settlement judgment, with complete cited cases. Programs are justified in cleared exceptions per analyst and reconciliation hours returned, not headcount removed.
How do you handle counterparty confidentiality?

Counterparty-scoped access on the retrieval index with logged reads, confidentiality enforced at the pipeline, and transfer governance as a build requirement. Sharing evidence with one counterparty never means exposing another's data.
What is the smallest program worth running?

One workflow, one baseline, one vertical slice — bordereaux reconciliation is the most common starter because the pain and the telemetry are both concrete. If the diagnostic cannot find the delta, we say so and stop.
Can the pricing build respect our actuarial judgment?

It is designed around it: the pipelines assemble data and run reproducible calculations, the actuaries own assumptions, judgment calls are recorded as structured rationale, and challengers run in the registry your model-risk function governs.
Who owns the build after you leave?

Your teams, with the runbooks, contracts, evaluation suites, the term library and registry entries transferred as gate conditions during expansion — not as a closing deliverable. Several programs run entirely in-house after the second quarter.
